sentences.text: Isla had heard the story of the storm since she was small and had heard it the way you hear a family story, which is to say in fragments, out of order, with the ending known before the beginning.

She got it properly in one go, on a wet afternoon in October, with a recorder on the table, because her school had set a local history project and Isla had realised on the bus that she was sitting on the best one in the county.
Her great-grandmother talked for fifty-one minutes and Isla did not interrupt once.
The storm came in on the second of February 1953 and it was, in that part of the country, the worst in a hundred years.
It is in the books.
There were people killed in it on the east coast and there was a ferry lost and the number is in every account of that winter.
At Cnoc Dubh there were fourteen houses in a hollow under the ridge, with a road in from the pass and nothing else.

Fourteen houses, sixty-one people, one telephone in the schoolroom that had gone with the line on the second night, and enough coal and meal in every house to sit out a fortnight without anybody thinking about it twice, because that was simply how you lived there in February.
That is the detail that people always miss, her great-grandmother said, and it is the one that matters most.
Nobody in that hollow was in trouble.
They were not running short and they were not frightened and they were not waiting to be found.
They were snowed in, in the ordinary way, in a place where being snowed in was a thing that happened most years and was chiefly a nuisance about the milk.
The road went on the first night.
That was normal; the road went most winters.

What was not normal was the second night, when the power line came down, and the third day, when the drifts across the mouth of the hollow were high enough that a man could walk over the top of a telegraph pole and one of them did, on purpose, to say he had.
By the fourth day the county had decided that Cnoc Dubh was a problem.
They sent a party from Ardmore, over the pass, thirteen men on foot with poles.
This is in the county record and Isla has since read the record, which is one paragraph long and extremely dry.
The party went over the pass on the morning of the fifth.
They came back to Ardmore that evening and reported that they had been unable to reach the settlement.
Isla found the actual wording in the county archive in Inverness, which took her two letters and a train.
*Party unable to reach Cnoc Dubh owing to conditions.
Returned 1740.* That is it.
Thirteen men, a full day on the hill in February, and one line.

She sat in the reading room and looked at it for a while and understood something about records that has stayed with her, which is that the paper is not the event; the paper is what somebody had the energy to write down at the end of a very long day.
They went again on the sixth, in better weather, with a local man who had been born in the hollow.
They came back and reported the same.
On the seventh an aircraft went over.
That is also in the record.
It flew the length of the glen at low level in clear conditions and reported no sign of the houses and no smoke.

And in the hollow, on the fifth, and the sixth, and the seventh, fourteen houses had their fires lit and their chimneys going and thirteen children were being made to do lessons at kitchen tables, and nobody in Cnoc Dubh had the faintest idea that anybody was looking for them.
